candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it. The Tycho supernova remnant as seen by the Chandra X-ray space telescope. candidates.title: Delivery Robot Causes Car Accident With Nine Injuries
candidates.raw_excerpt: At least nine bus riders were injured when a wayward delivery robot plowed into oncoming traffic in Estonia. The incident happened in the capital city Tallinn, in the middle of rush-hour traffic. As Estonian public broadcaster ERR reported , a delivery robot operated by the company Starship Technologies blundered into an intersection during a “no walk” signal, bringing it squarely into the path of an oncoming bus. Reacting to the obstacle darting out into the road, the bus driver hit the brakes, sending passengers tumbling. The driver’s quick reaction might have actually spared the robot, as the device reportedly continued on its delivery route after colliding with the front of the bus. “The robot fled, if you can put it that way,” as one Tallinn Transport official told ERR . As the spokesperson put it, the robot’s actions may legally constitute fleeing the scene of a traffic incident, meaning Starship Technologies could very well be on the hook for the incident. “If a participant in a traffic accident leaves the scene without fulfilling the obligations prescribed by law, this may constitute an offense,” the transportation official explained. It wouldn’t the company’s first brush with the law. In Arizona, a 73-year-old woman is suing the company after one of its robots allegedly pushed her to the ground, ramming into her repeatedly as she tried to get up. As for the Estonian situation, Starship’s head of operation Pepe Aaviksoo blamed bright ad boards and traffic lights, which apparently disoriented the robot’s sensors. “There are many lessons to be learned, but exceptional situations do occur,” he said. candidates.raw_excerpt: Tuesdays midterm elections in the US were a referendum on a lot of things — the war on Iran , data centers , and the ultra-powerful tech lobby , to name just a few. In several local contests, the elections were also a crushing blow for the rising domestic surveillance industry , as voters sent automatic license plate reader (ALPR) companies like Flock Safety packing. In York County, Maine, for example, a ballot measure to remove the town’s current ALPRs and require voter approval for any future installations of surveillance technology passed with flying colors, winning a 72 percent share of the vote. And in League City, Texas, a measure to “advise the city to continue police use” of ALPRs failed — albeit by a slimmer margin, with 54 percent of voters opposing the measure. As the newspaper Community Impact reported , cities like Pflugerville, Texas also passed ordinances requiring public approval before installing any facial recognition, surveillance, and AI tools that could infringe on residents’ privacy going forward. Beyond ballot measures, municipal politicians with wishy-washy messaging around Flock bans were also trounced. candidates.raw_excerpt: Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world. The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 5, 2002: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by Jupiter moon Amalthea only to find it's a 'pile of icy rubble less dense than water'
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft was almost out of fuel. But the Jupiter mission still had some science to do. Galileo flew by a small moon called Amalthea. Amalthea is small, but it's interesting for scientists. The Jupiter moon Amalthea is the reddest object in our solar system. It also generates more heat than it gets from the sun. Scientists think Amalthea creates electrical currents as it orbits in Jupiter's huge magnetic field. Near this little moon, strong radiation from Jupiter is dangerous for spacecraft. The flyby caused some problems for Galileo. The spacecraft went into safe mode only 30 minutes after going past Amalthea. NASA said it was ready for problems, because Galileo was on its last legs, and the radiation near Amalthea was strong. However, NASA quickly fixed the problem and got Galileo working again. Less than a year later, Galileo threw itself into Jupiter's atmosphere . The spacecraft was crushed by the high pressure in Jupiter's atmosphere, but its data still survives on Earth. The Jupiter moon Amalthea as seen by NASA's Galileo spacecraft on Nov. 5, 2002. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Why it mattered The Galileo spacecraft was running on cosmic fumes by the time it reached Amalthea and the flyby would be the last time the probe would ever swing by one of Jupiter's moons . While it may not look like it in Galileo's black and white images above and below, Amalthea is tinted red due sulfur contamination on its surface. The moon is small, about 168 miles long, and orbits about 112,468 miles (181,000 km) from Jupiter (much closer to the planet than the Earth and its moon). Galileo flew within 99 miles of Amalthea during its flyby, which also marked the closest Galileo would get to Jupiter before its death dive in September 2005. Voyager 1 is almost one light-day from Earth, meaning that a command takes nearly a day to reach the spacecraft and a response takes another day to come back to our planet. The spacecraft will reach the light-day milestone on Nov. 18, at 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth. NASA's Deep Space Network of three antennas does check-ins to make sure the spacecraft is doing well. On Oct. 18 and 19, Voyager 1 did not respond. Its signal fortunately reappeared on Oct. 20. "Engineers still are investigating what caused the communication loss," JPL added in the statement, but said it appears Voyager 1 went into a sort of safe mode. "The team has so far determined that one group of thrusters went offline and their backups turned on. Such a swap is programmed to occur automatically if the spacecraft computers detect something amiss with the active thrusters." Voyager 1 and its still-operational twin, Voyager 2 , both launched in 1977 on an initial mission to explore planets in the solar system. candidates.title: Chinese researchers study design measurements for lunar buildings
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Chinese researchers are working on a set of proposed design measurements for future buildings on the moon.

On Earth, architects use design guidelines and common measurements for buildings, from ceiling heights and aisle widths to doorframe dimensions. According to the researchers, those measurements might be drastically different on the moon.

"Buildings on the moon and on Earth will certainly be different, and the differences will be huge," Han Chenping, a professor at the School of Architecture and Design at the China University of Mining and Technology, told CGTN recently in Beijing.

One of the biggest differences between the moon and Earth is gravity. Gravity on the moon's surface is about one-sixth as strong as gravity on Earth.

"People's way of moving, their behavior, and their body dimensions inside such buildings will be different," Han said.

Those differences mean future lunar living could benefit from a new set of reference measurements, which Han's team hopes to develop.

For now, the team has calculated a possible height for steps in lunar buildings. The team's estimate is roughly twice the height of a typical step on Earth. Han said the estimate takes into account not just how high people might be able to step in lower gravity, but also how well they can maintain their balance.

The team says developing such measurements is difficult, as lunar conditions are hard to simulate on Earth. The measurements would also need to be tested on the moon.

The team hopes that developing such proposed guidelines could provide reference measurements for future lunar buildings. "To make future living and working spaces on the moon safe, comfortable and efficient. " Han said.

Han presented the team's research on common dimensions for lunar buildings at the recent International Astronautical Congress in Türkiye.

Today's spacewalk will wrap up an ambitious ISS power upgrade that has taken more than five years to pull off. "The installation job will complete the years-long process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts," NASA officials wrote about the EVA in a blog post on Tuesday (Nov. 3) . candidates.title: Chinese scientists envision the first road on the moon
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Chinese scientists are working to design roads on the moon.

One concept, put forward by a team from Beihang University, envisions a road built from crushed stone that is excavated in situ or sintered on the moon — quite similar to gravel roads on Earth.

"Modern roads began as gravel surfaces, so I think the moon's first road could start the same way," Li Feng, a professor at Beihang University's School of Transportation Science and Engineering, told CGTN.

The moon's environment differs from Earth's — with temperature differences of up to 300 degrees Celsius and a different gravity environment — but the team believes the moon's first roads should meet the same standards: level, solid, durable, economical and feasible.

Li says their goal was to make the technology feasible within 5 to 10 years.

"I think one advantage of our concept is that it's technically more mature, because you don't need to bake large bricks — you only need small crushed stones, either sintered or excavated in situ," Li added.

The team has carried out related research using lunar samples gathered from China's Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 missions.

They have named their conceptual lunar road the moon's "Qinzhidao". The Qinzhidao is generally regarded as ancient China's earliest "highway", built more than 2,200 years ago during the Qin Dynasty.

"We want to pay tribute to that road in ancient China," Li says.

The study was published in January 2026 in the China Journal of Highway and Transport.

candidates.title: Farewell Swift
candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered this morning, bringing the 22-year-old mission to an end. NASA contracted with Katalyst Space in September 2025 to revamp an existing system to try and rescue Swift after increased solar activity caused it to lose altitude sooner than expected. In less than nine months, Katalyst launched their LINK spacecraft to grapple Swift, but attitude control problems scuttled the effort. Swift reentered at 7:39 am EST today over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia at approximately 3.4º N latitude, 98.6ºE degrees longitude. Launched in 2004, Swift studied gamma-ray bursts. With three multiwavelength telescopes, Swift looked at the universe in the visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma-ray bands. In 2017, NASA named it in honor of Neil Gehrels, Swift’s Principal Investigator, after he passed away. Last fall when it became clear increased solar activity would cause Swift to reenter sooner than expected, NASA contracted with Katalyst for $30 million to launch a rescue mission using its LINK spacecraft even though Swift wasn’t designed to be reboosted and didn’t have grappling fixtures. Katalyst’s Kieren Wilson called it an “unprepared but cooperative partner,” good at pointing. The name Swift refers to its ability to quickly repoint itself when a gamma ray burst is detected so the other instruments can study it in the X-ray and UV bands. LINK launched on a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket from Kwajalein Atoll in the Pacific on July 3, 2026 , but soon encountered problems . An unresponsive Reaction Control System (RCS) valve caused LINK to spin up and then a power circuit switch failure doomed the effort. Today NASA credited Swift with broadening “our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system.”

candidates.title: Viasat, SES, and Astranis Win NASA Ka-band Relay Contracts
candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA awarded contracts to Viasat , SES , and Astranis for Ka-band space relay capability concepts, as part of the Space Communications and Navigation (SCaN) program’s Communications Services Project (CSP). Viasat received the largest contract award for $460.9 million. Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. (which is SES Space & Defense) was contracted for $340.4 million, and Astranis was contracted for $264.3 million. The awards are firm-fixed-price contracts, but NASA has the option to award additional funding to advance the work from capability concepts to in-orbit flight demonstrations. The work period runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029. This is part of NASA’s work to replace the aging Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) fleet with commercial services for future missions. TDRS provides information relay services to the International Space Station, Hubble Space Telescope, and other missions. TDRS is expected to support its current missions into the mid-2030s, but it stopped onboarding new missions in late 2024 . According to NASA’s solicitation for the contracts, NASA intends to acquire an end-to-end Ka-band relay service that is backward-compatible with legacy TDRSS users for at least 15 years. The Broad Agency Announcement (BAA) details three phases: a first 6-month phase for concept maturation and risk reduction; an option for up to two years of system integration, flight demonstration and capability verification and validation; and a third option for up to six months of additional demonstration, anomaly resolution, and service validation. Both SES and Viasat received contracts in 2022 when NASA started the CSP to explore future commercial options for TDRS.
